I have an extremely controversial opinion about the Navier-Stokes debate going on.

What if @OpenAI actually does deserve some of the credit?

The story is that OpenAI stole Tristan Buckmaster's research and used it to create their own proof of what he was working on.

But how? How did they steal his research?

The more you dig you'll find that OpenAI had access to Buckmaster's research because he was using an AI agentic service called Codex. I'm a computer scientist. I write code all the time but never with GenAI. I'd never heard of Codex so I looked it up.

Codex is software built around OpenAIs LLM, ChatGPT.

It's an agentic AI. It is generative AI for scientists.

If you look through my posts you'll know I am absolutely vicious towards those who vibe code. Vibe coding is for wannabes who don't want to put in the work to actually learn how to code. I will NEVER be impressed by a vibe coder because they didn't actually do anything.

The AI did it for you.....

That's my problem with AI. People rely on it so much that they don't actually end up doing anything. They'll take the credit for building an entire software platform but they didn't actually do anything. They asked an AI to do it. That was the end of their efforts. The AI did the actual work.

Morally, that is a pretty simple situation when it comes to building software. If you did something with the help of GenAI then you didn't actually do it.

It has always been my viewpoint that if a person uses AI to vibe code an app I am giving 100% of the credit for that app to the AI since the AI actually did the work.

You see where I'm going with this?

Codex is a coding platform not with ChatGPT built in but with ChatGPT as its foundation. Codex is built around ChatGPT.

Codex.... is essentially a very advanced form of input for GenAI to generate things like code and mathematical formulae for the end user.

So........

For months I have been proclaiming on this platform that if you used AI to do it then you didn't actually do it. The AI did.

That's a pretty simple situation when it comes to something as mundane as general use software.

But a vibe coded mathematical proof to a millennium prize problem? That's on a whole different level.

How much work did Buckmaster actually do and how much was vibe coded?

If credit for a generated software platform goes to the generative AI then shouldn't the credit for a generated proof also go to the AI?

If Buckmaster were forced to redo everything he's claiming credit for but this time without the use of GenAI in any way, shape, or form could he do it?

Who actually deserves the credit here?

You continue to naively believe in the outdated mantra that technology always only creates new jobs.

While the economy of 2028 without people is approaching step by step.

Where the world's first billion-dollar company may consist of just one founder and hundreds of autonomous agents.

For the first time in human history, artificial intelligence is replacing not muscles or routine work, but human thinking, analytics and decision-making.

While millions of white-collar workers continue to entertain the illusion of irreplaceability, the term of full agent autonomy doubles every few months, blurring the line between human and software.

This process triggers a terrible economic loop: companies hire fewer people, the unemployed consume fewer goods, and businesses buy even more artificial intelligence to protect their own margins and profits.

This entire irreversible transformation brings us to the main existential question of our century: when machines begin to do absolutely all the work without the slightest human intervention, colossal trillions of dollars in profit will go not to those who went to work every day, but exclusively to those in whose hands the ownership of these machines is concentrated.

Award-winning actor Elijah Canlas is drawing a hard line against the controversial US-led Pax Silica initiative.

Canlas expressed his frustrations regarding the proposed AI and critical mineral processing hub, speaking out against policies that prioritize unchecked innovation over the welfare of Indigenous and marginalized sectors.

"It's bad. I feel like they should not legislate it. Nobody should support it," Canlas said in an interview following the press conference of his new film "Edjop." 

Led by the United States, the Pax Silica initiative, which aims to "secure global supply chains for artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and critical minerals" will be a 4,000-acre high-tech industrial and innovation hub that has been proposed for New Clark City in Tarlac.

"Ang daming maaabusong environmental resources, ang daming maaabusong mga komunidad. Talo talaga tayong taumbayan."

While the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), alongside implementers in the Philippine government tout that the massive zone could generate over 130,000 jobs and pull billions in investments, artificial intelligence and manufacturing advancements, Canlas called out the repetitive nature of these promises.

He dismissed the long-touted benefits of similar past initiatives as "mga hoax lang for the past few decades."

"So I think it's very clear. For me, it's weird that people support it, for me," he remarked.

Canlas did acknowledge the perspective of those pushing for modernization, but he remained resolute that the heavy trade-offs are completely unjustified. "Pero there are so many other factors… marami kang masa-sacrifice. Parang hindi worth it, 'di ba?"

In earlier news, scientist coalition AGHAM-Advocates of Science and Technology for the People has debunked the claims of the BCDA on the alleged national technological development benefits the Pax Silica initiative "will bring."

“Walang nakasulat dito na technology transfer. Walang nakasulat dito na magiging sa atin 'yong mga technologies na nandiyan. Tayo ay magpaparenta lang ng lupa, tayo ay pupuntahan nila para i-process dito 'yong mga minerals dito pero iiwan din sa atin ang mga waste,” AGHAM spox Giovanni Tapang said to media.

A proud Artista ng Bayan who studied in the Philippine High School for the Arts and University of the Philippines Manila, Canlas is Edgar Jopson in the upcoming biopic "Edjop," alongside Jodi Sta. Maria, Kakie Pangilinan, Menchu Lauchengco-Yulo, Nour Hooshmand, Cedrick Juan, Issa Litton, and Teroy Guzman, directed by Katski Flores.

Drawing from accounts, recordings, and interviews with the Jopson family, "Edjop" follows the fragmented memories of his daughter Joyette in recounting the life of the Ateneo student activist-turned-Red fighter who was instrumental in sparking the First Quarter Storm, a series of protests in the 1970s that led to the downfall of the Marcos Sr. regime. The film is set to open in cinemas nationwide on September 16.

(✍️: Rafael Asonza)

tweets.text:
From Importing Technology to Helping Design It

❓ Is #Oman beginning to establish a position within the global semiconductor value chain?

US semiconductor and connectivity company [Movandi] is establishing a research and development centre in Muscat focused on smart communications and artificial intelligence.

The centre is expected to work with Omani universities and research institutions to co-develop technologies and build local capabilities.

Movandi develops semiconductor and connectivity solutions for (5G), emerging (6G) networks, data centres, drones, robotics and artificial-intelligence infrastructure.

Oman’s technology investment group [ITHCA] previously led a ($20 million) investment in Movandi as part of a wider ($40 million) funding round.

Its semiconductor-related investments also include:

◼️ Around (OMR 5 million) in chip-design company [GSME].

◼️ Around (OMR 1.93 million) in programmable-optics company [Lumotive].

Beyond the News:

Entering the semiconductor industry does not necessarily begin with building large and costly fabrication plants.

Economic value also exists in chip design, intellectual property, software, testing, research and specialised engineering—areas where Oman could gradually build a competitive presence.

The real measure of success will not be the number of technology companies attracted, but how much knowledge, research, engineering employment and exportable technology remains and develops inside Oman.
